cells.remarks: (Vaṭṭeluttu.) On a slab built into the same floor. A record in the sixteenth year of the Pāṇḍya king Varaguṇa- Mahārāja. Records gift of money. The village is called Ilaṅgōkkuḍi. From his camp at Araśūr on the Peṇṇār in Toṇḍanāḍu he granted 290 kāśus to the temple of Tiruppōttuḍaiyār at Ilaṅgōkkuḍi in Muḷḷināḍu. The village assembly received the money and the savai vāriyar or committee of the assembly and the temple servants had jointly to provide for offerings to the God, according to a fixed scale, from the interest on the 290 kāśus. Veṅkayya identifies the king with the celebrated Varaguṇa Pāṇḍya who came to throne in A.D. 862. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IX, pp. 84—94. Here Veṅkayya discusses the king's expedition against Iḍavai and Vembil north of the Kāvēri, his battle with the combined army of Aparājita and Pṛithvīpati I at Tiruppirambiyam, and points out that this should have been in the course of a campaign against Aparājita which took him as far as Araśūr. As for the date of these Veṅkayya points out on the authority of the Aivarmalai inscription that his stay at Araśūr should have been in A.D. 877- 878, his campaign against Vembil in 872-3, and the battle of Tiruppirambiyam in 877-8 or next year. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IX, p. 88.

cells.remarks: On the same wall. A record in the thirty-third year of the Pāṇḍya king Māravarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulachēkharadēva (1268—1308), “ who was pleased to take every country.” Registers a gift by the artisans (kaṇmālar) of Kalladaikurichchi alias Kshatriyasikhāmaṇipuram to the shrine of the Goddess in the temple of Nālayira-Īśvaramuḍaiya-Nāyanār. The English equivalent of the date (Mithuna 12, New Moon, Mrigaśīrsha) was June 7, A.D. 1301, Wednesday. Mr. Sewell infers from this that the outer limits for the king's accession should be June 8 and June 27 of 1268.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 9 of 1913 (called the Veḷḷāṅguḍi plates of Veṅkaṭa I).—A record, dated in Ś. 1520, Viḷambi, in the time of Emperor Veṅkaṭapati I, making the gift, to several Brahmans, of the village of Veḷḷāṅguḍi, the hamlet of Kaḷḷaḍaikurichchi, renamed Vīrabhūpasamudram, in Muḷḷi-nāḍu in Tiruvaḍi dēśa. cells.remarks: On the south wall of the same shrine. Records in the eighth year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Konerinmaikondan gift of land at Sevval to the same temple for repairs and for worship, with the permission of Pammiyakkan. The land was made tax-free (iraiyili) by the king at the request of Gangeyarayan, chief of Tunjalur. Built in at the end. See note to the next epigraph.

cells.remarks: On the same wall. Records in the ninth year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Konerinmaikondan (Maravarman Sundara Pandya II) that Tiruppullanidasar of Servanmahadevi-chaturvedimangalam, having built the temple of Kanaviniya-Perumal, a certain Pammiyakkan endowed it with the necessary land (nattam) required for temple buildings, gardens, and the Brahmana village called Tentiruvayottiyai. At the request of Gangeyarayan, chief of Tunjalur, the king made the nattam under reference, tax-free (iraiyili). At the end of this record is engraved another of the eighth year of the king, which refers to the same temple and to the Brahmana village Tentiruvayottiyai-vilagam. [Mr. Krishna Sastri believes that Pammiyakkan was probably the mother of Sundara Pandya and sister of the Hoysala king Virasomesvara.]

text.remarks: On the same wall. Records in the ninth year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Konerinmaikondan (Maravarman Sundara Pandya II) that Tiruppullanidasar of Servanmahadevi-chaturvedimangalam, having built the temple of Kanaviniya-Perumal, a certain Pammiyakkan endowed it with the necessary land (nattam) required for temple buildings, gardens, and the Brahmana village called Tentiruvayottiyai. At the request of Gangeyarayan, chief of Tunjalur, the king made the nattam under reference, tax-free (iraiyili). At the end of this record is engraved another of the eighth year of the king, which refers to the same temple and to the Brahmana village Tentiruvayottiyai-vilagam. [Mr. Krishna Sastri believes that Pammiyakkan was probably the mother of Sundara Pandya and sister of the Hoysala king Virasomesvara.]

cells.remarks: A C.P. grant of the Vijayanagara king Venkata II, in Sanskrit verse and Nandinagari character. Records that on the full-moon day of Vaisakha of S. 1556 (A.D. 1634-5), Bhava, Vira Venkatapati Maharaya granted to a number of Brahmans the village of Kuniyur or Muttukrishnapuram in the Viravanallur Magana in Mulli-nadu, Tiruvadirajya. The inscription gives not only the pedigree of the last Vijayanagara dynasty but also that of the feudatory Madura Naiks. The inscription was issued by the great Tirumal Naik who thus in 1634 acknowledged his suzerain. See Ep. Rep. 1891, p. 6, and Ep. Ind., Vol. III, pp. 236-58. See also my History of the Naik kingdom of Madura in Ind. Antq., November 1916, p. 185.

cells.remarks: On the east wall of the same prākāra. A damaged record of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Vīra-Pāṇḍyadēva, "who having taken Īḷam (Ceylon), Koṅgu and Soḷa-maṇḍalam, conquered the powerful chiefs and was pleased to perform the anointment of heroes and victors at Perumbarṟappuliyūr," dated sixteenth year. Registers the gift mentioned in No. 100 and perhaps also another gift of land to supplement it under the orders of the assembly of Śēravanmahādēvi-chaturvēdimaṅgalam. The taxes on this land are stated to have been deducted in the account (puravu-vari) registers. The Government Epigraphist believes that this king might be the Jaṭāvarman Vīra-Pāṇḍya who, according to professor Kielhorn, came to the throne in 1253. Among the taxes are enumerated the kaḍamai, antaṟāyam, viniyōgam, achchavari, kāriyavārārchi, veṭṭippāṭṭam, pañchupīli, sandhivikrakappēṟu, vāsalpēṟu, ilāñjiṅaikpēṟu, uḻuḏāṅkuḏi, pāḍikkāval, ponvari, etc.

cells.remarks: (Vaṭṭeḷuttu.) On the same wall. A damaged record of the Chōla-Pāṇḍya king Māravarman alias Uḍaiyār-Śrī- Vikrama-Chōla-Pāṇḍyadēva, dated twentieth year. Mentions Ādanūr in Śūraṅguḍi-nāḍu, which was a subdivision of Muḍigoṇḍa- Chōlavalanaḍu in Rājarāja-Pāṇḍināḍu and seems to record a gift of lamps. At the top of this inscription is an incomplete line in Vaṭṭeḷuttu characters which refers to the third year of Jaṭāvarman alias Sundara-Chōla-Pāṇḍyadēva. [The political divisions were evidently named after Rājēndra Chōla I (Muḍigoṇḍa) and Rājarāja I. The Government Epigraphist surmises that Vikrama was the successor of the Viceroy Sundara Chōla-Pāṇḍya, their mutual relationship being unknown.]

cells.remarks: On the same wall. Dated in the thirteenth year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Kōnērimēlkoṇḍān and 1119th day. Records that a few specified villages clubbed together as Sundarapāṇḍya-chaturvēdimangalam received the new name Uttamaśōla-chaturvēdimangalam after that of the grandson (pēra nār) Uttamaśōjan-pēraraiyar and was granted to the temple of Uttamaśōla-vinnagar-Ālvār. [Mr. Krishna Sastri surmises that Kōnērinmaikoṇḍān might be the son of Uttamaśōla who was the son of Prince Sundara Pāṇḍya referred to in 265. The inscription says that the villages suffered from famine and heavy taxation, that people deserted, lands remained uncultivated and temple wor ship ceased; that the king was then petitioned to and he reclaimed them once again, changing the name of the villages and deity to that of his father (?) Uttamaśōla.]

cells.remarks: In his Antiquities Mr. Sewell gives twelve inscriptions in the place, the dates of some of which are probably inaccurate. Four of these are dated in K.Ā. 689, K.Ā. 552 (?), K.A. 552 ? and K.A. 685 and record grants by Māṟtaṇḍavarman while residing in the "Vīra Pāṇḍyan palace" at this place. One inscription, dated K.Ā. 575 (A.D. 1399), records grant of lands to temple by Karamani Appan. The next three records, dated in K.Ā. 680, K.Ā. 697, and K.Ā. 697, are also grants by Māṟtaṇḍavarma. Three records of the same sovereign are in Gōmati Amman temple and dated in K.Ā. 707, K.Ā. 721 and K.Ā. 721. The last of the series is an inscription of K.Ā. 721 in Chaṇḍīśvar Amman temple. [See Antiquities, p. 314.].

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 167 of Mr. Sewell's List.--Records a sale date by the chief of Vannikūḍam in the Tinnevelly district of certain lands to the Tinnevelly temple. The name of the chief is not mentioned. But it is stated that the sale was undertaken in order to increase the merit (punniyattukkāha) of Raṅga Kṛishṇa Muttu Vīrappa Nāyakka (1682--9) and Tiruveṅgaṉātha Ayyar. The Kollam Āṇḍu 858 is given, and the year Durmukhi. [Tiruveṅga nātha was the celebrated Maḍai Tiruveṅgaḍanāthaiyar of Tamil literary tradition, the translator of the Prabōdhachandrōdayam into Tamil.]

cells.remarks: On the same wall. A record of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Vīra- Pāṇḍyadēva, "who took Īlam (Ceylon), Koṅgu and Sōṇāḍu and was pleased to perform the anointment of heroes at Perumbarrappuliyūr," dated in his fourteenth year. Mentions Śrī-Posala-Vīra-Sōmidēva-chaturvēdimangalam, a brahmadēya in Murappunāḍu and a matha in it. Refers to a sale made in the eleventh year (of the king's reign). [Mr. T. A. Gopinatha Rao identifies this king with the Vīra Pāṇḍya of the rock inscription of the Sthāṇunātha temple at Suchindram, "who conquered the Malaināḍu." He argues, on the basis of a similar institution at Tirukkadavūr (Tanjore district) that this king was the contemporary of Rājādhirāja (II) and Kulōttuṅga (III), and that he was closely related by marriage with the Kēraḷa or Kūpaka king at Kollam. See Trav. Arch. Ser. (II, 15 - 21) for details. Mr. Krishna Sastri, however, points out that as the Hoysaḷa Vīra Sōmēśvara, the uncle of Sundara Pāṇḍya (II, 1239-51) is referred to, king Vīra Pāṇḍya should have been later and was probably identical with the king who, according to Kielhorn, had the initial date 1253. See Shermādēvi inscriptions.]

cells.remarks: On the west and south walls of the same shrine. A record in the thirty-third year of the Pāṇḍya king Māravarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Śrīvallabhadēva regarding the claim of a certain priest in the temple of Iruvarku-Īśvaramuḍaiya-Nāyanār at Ilañji alias Sundara-Pāṇḍyanallūr in Tenvārināḍu which had been overlooked by the king's elder brother on account of the priest's absence from the place and distributed among three others. [Was the king the same as he who came to the throne in 1258 ?]

cells.remarks: On a quadrangular pillar set up in the same place. cells.remarks: On the wall, right of entrance into the central shrine of the Venkatachalapati temple. cells.remarks: On the same wall, left of entrance. A record of the Vijayanagara king Vira-Sadasivadeva-Maharaya in S. 1485, Krodhana (wrong). Records gift of the villages Ariyakulam, Puttaneri alias Tiruvenqadanallur, Pottaikulam, Kodikkulam, Kuttukkal, Siramankulam and some land in Alikudi to the temple of Tiruvenqadanathadeva by Krishnappa Nayaka of the Kasyapa-gotra. It is stated that the latter had acquired the Tiruvadidesa in which these villages were situated, as amaranayakam from Ramarajar-Ayyan. [Krishnappa was the son and successor of Visvanatha I, the founder of the Naik dynasty of Madura. For a detailed account of his reign see Ind. Antq., 1916, p. 82 ff.]

cells.remarks: (Vaṭṭeluttu.) On one of the pillars in the Ambalavānasvāmin temple. Dated in the reign of the Pāṇḍya king Mārañjaḍaiyan (whom the Government Epigraphist attributes to the ninth century). Registers in his thirty-fifth year and four hundred and sixty-ninth day an agreement of the Mahāsabhā of Maṇanilainallūr, a brahmadēya in Kaḷakkūḍi-nāḍu. [The inscription is of invaluable interest and describes the rules of membership in the sabhā. See Ep. Rep., 1913, p. 98, where a full summary is given. It is too long to be quoted here.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 10 of Mr. Sewell's List.— Records grant of twelve villages in the Tinnevelly district by Viśvanātha Nāyakka (1559— 1563), the first of the great Nāyakka dynasty of Madura, and his celebrated minister and general Aryanātha, who built the thousandpillared maṇṭapam at Madura. The former is styled "the pious son of Kotyam Nāgama Nāyuḍu;" the latter "Mandaraputtangēri Ārya Nāyaka Muḍaliyār." The grant is in Ś. 1482 (A.D. 1560), Raudri. For a full account of Viśvanātha and Aryanātha, see Ind. Antq., 1914-5.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 56 of Mr. Sewell’s List.--Records grant of a house by certain persons to a female belonging to the Śiva temple in Tinnevelly for the maintenance of worship, in Ś. 1653 (A.D. 1731), K.A. 907, Virōdhikrit, in the reign of Vijaya Raṅga Chokkanātha (1705--31), of the Nāyakka dynasty of Madura. It is noticeable that, though the grant is for a Śiva temple, the deed is ornamented with [Footnote 1] 188 Vaishnava figures, the engraver being a worshipper of Vishnu, as appears from his name Anavattan Perumal.

cells.remarks: On the outside of the east wall of the third prakara of the Nelliyappar temple. A record of the Pandya king Sundara-Pandyadeva. [The Pandya king referred to is Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I, 1251--64.]

cells.remarks: On the outside of the east wall of the second prākāra of the same temple, right of entrance. A record in the thirteenth year of the Pandya king Kō-Jaṭāvarman Kulēśkharadēva (I, 1190-1217). Records gift of land. See Ep. Ind., Vol. VI, p. 302, where Dr. Kielhorn points out that the date of this inscription (Thursday, Pūrvāshādha, Aparapak. 4, Mina 4th) corresponds to 26th February 1204. [This is in agreement with the date of the larger Tiruppūvanam grant of the same king and establishes the fact that the king came to the throne in the period between 27th February and 29th November 1190.]

cells.remarks: On the east wall of the shrine of Jñānapiran in the temple of Ādinātha. Dated in the fourth year of the Pāṇḍya king Māravarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulaśēkharadēva. Records gift of the two villages of Seṅgaṅkuļam and Neḍuṅguļam, hamlets of Tirukkurugūr in Tiruvaļudivaļanāḍu, by a certain Ōḍanāttadigal for feeding the learned men of the "eighteen (Vaishṇava) countries" who met in the Aruļāļadāsa-matha founded by himself in the temple of Poliñjiṇinraruļiya Paramasvāmi at Tirukkurugūr. Mentions Śrī-vaikunḍam alias Rājēndra-chaturvēdimangalam, Tiruvāymoļimāmuni, a disciple of Tirukkurugūrmāmuni, and the palace of the king situated in a grove south of Jayangoṇḍaśōlapuram. [Mr. Krishna Sastri points out that the unusual nature of the king's introduction prevents his being identified with Māravarman Kulaśēkhara I and thinks that he was perhaps the contemporary and successor of Jaṭāvarman Śrīvallabha.] See Ep. Rep., 1910, p. 99.

cells.remarks: (Vaṭṭeḷuttu.) On two slabs set up in the Subrahmanya temple. A record in the thirteenth year of the Pāṇḍya king Varaguṇa-Māraya. The inscription was partially copied in 1903. Registers that the king who was a devotee of [Footnote *] An extensive Tamil poem purporting to be the translation of a Sanskrit Purāṇa on this place, consisting of ten adhyāyas and 898 viruttas, exists. Its author is Veṇṟimalai Kavirāya, a servant of the shrine. He lived perhaps in the eighteenth century. Subrahmanya Bhatāra provided 1,400 gold coins (kāsus) for the requirements of the temple throughout the twelve months of the year. The money was distributed among sixteen villages which were required only to pay interest at two kalams of paddy per year on each kāsu borrowed, without disturbing principal. (Note the rate of interest.)

cells.remarks: On a pillar set up in the same place. A record in the thirteenth year of the Pandya king Māravarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kōnermaikoṇḍān Vikrama- Pāṇḍyadeva. Records gift of two māis of land at Maṅgalakkurichchi in Tiruvaḷudīvalaṅādu to a Brāhmaṇa of Parākrama-Pāṇḍyachaturvedimaṅgalam in Karuṅguḍi-nāḍu. [The king may be identical with him who came to the throne in A.D. 1282 and was the conqueror of Vīragaṇḍa Gopāla and Gaṇapati. Mr. Krishna Sastri, however, believes that he was perhaps a contemporary of Arikēsari Parākrama, founder of the Teṅkāśi temple, as Kaliyugarāman was.]

cells.remarks: On the same pillar. Records in K.A. 621, sale of land mentioned in No. 27, to Narkīradēva Nāyanār in the temple of Subrahmanya-Piḷḷaiyār at Tiruchchendil, for 630 Kaliyugarāman-paṇam (named after Vīra Pāṇḍya, the contemporary of Arikēsari Parākrama). It is stated that this land which was at Maṅgalakkurichchi alias Peruṅkarunai-chaturvēdimaṅgalam was originally granted to the Brāhmaṇa Attigirinātha- Bhaṭṭar and two others of Parākramapāṇḍya-chaturvedimaṅgalam by Raṇaraṅgarāma-Perumāl alias Vikrama-Pāṇḍyadeva. [The dedication of a shrine to Nakkīra shows the importance attached in the age to literary greatness. Nakkīrar was one of the last Saṅgam poets and was the author of the Tirumurugāṟṟuppaḍai and Irayanār-agapporuḷ. For an account of his life see Abhidhānachintāmaṇi, p. 572.]

cells.remarks: On the south wall of the garbhagriha in the Paśupatīśvara temple. A record in the fourth year of the Chōla king Kō-Rājakēsarivarman alias Uḍaiyār Śrī-Vīra-Rājēndradēva (I, 1064--70) granting the village of Pakkūr in Veṅgala nāḍu in Adhirājarāja maṇḍalam to the shrine. It gives a graphic account of Vīra Rājēndra's three wars with the Western Chālukyan Āhavamalla Sōmēśvara I and his two sons Vikramāditya VI and Jayasimha III and their Sāmantas Chavuṇḍarāya, Kēśavāditya and Narasimha. The battle of Kūḍal-saṅgam is said to have given the Chōla decisive victory. See Ibid., p. 50. Also S.I.I., Vol. III, pp. 31--9, where Dr. Hultzsch edits the inscription.

cells.remarks: In the same place. A record in the third year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Kōṇērimēḷkoṇḍān. Records the grant of certain privileges to temple servants. At their marriages and funerals double conches might be blown and drums beaten. They could build two storeys for their houses, could cover them with plaster, could have double doors therein, and decorate their outside with garlands of water-lilies. [The inscription is very interesting for the mention of restrictions even in regard to house buildings.]

cells.remarks: On the south wall of the central shrine in the Choleśvara temple. Records in the fourth year of the Chōla king Rājakēsarivarman alias Udaiyar Rājēndra-Chōladēva (i.e., Rājēndra Chōla II, later on Kulōttuṅga I) gift of land to the temple of Madhurāntaka-Īśvaramudaiyar also called Śrī- Kailāsa. The land was purchased from the sabhā of Sōjakulamāṇikka-chaturvēdimangalam, a brahmadēya in Ādanūr-nādu (a subdivision) of Abhimānajīva-valaṇādu. [Contains also an incomplete inscription of the fifth year of Parakēsarivarman alias Udaiyar Rājēndra-Chōladēva.] Mr. Venkayya points out that the usurper's power extended into the Chōla country by this year, that his war with Ādhi Rājēndra must have taken place subsequent to this and been followed by the Western Chālukyan invasion of the Chōla country. Ep. Rep., 1904, p. 12.

cells.remarks: [For the history of this Pālayam see Trichinopoly Gazr., p. 283.] Epigraphically the place has been noticed for five old copper-plate grants in the possession of the Zemindar; ‘ but the first three of these are absolutely valueless, as two of them are dated in 912 and the third in 1195 A.D., while it is obvious that the estate cannot be as ancient as this. They mix up Chōlas, Pāṇḍyas, Nayakkans and poligars in inextricable confusion. The other two grants are dated in 1747 and 1783 and apparently record gifts of lands to certain temples. The latter contains a long list of the poligars, but gives no dates for them.” (Trichinopoly Gazr., p. 283.)

cells.remarks: On the south and east walls of the same shrine. Dated in the reign of the Vijayanagara king Sadāśivadēva Mahārāya, son of Achyutarāya. Records in Ś. 1466, expired, Krōdhin, Mithuna, ba. di. 10, Rēvati, Friday (details not enough for calculation), a gift of land in Kuḷiṟṟalai-śīrmai alias Karuṅgilappaḷli in Mikōḍu-nāḍu, a subdivision of Teṅkarai- Rājagambhīra-vala-nāḍu, by Tirumappa Nāyaka (son of Siṅgama Naik and grandson of Koṇḍama Naik), an agent of Rāmarāja-Chinna- Tammayadēva-Mahārāja, for the morning offerings in the temple of Tirumanikka-malai-udaiya-Tambiranar. Ramaraja Chinna Tammayadeva was a member of the Aravīti family and like his brother Viṭṭhala was the cousin-brother of the great minister Rāma Rāya. Timma accompanied his brother Viṭṭhala in his southern campaign of 1545.

cells.remarks: On the same rock. Dated in the reign of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Sundara-Pāṇḍyadēva (I, 1251—64). The king settled the dispute between the trustees of this temple and the nagarattār of Śivapādaśēkharapuram as regards the payment of taxes (kaḍamai) by the people residing in the vicinity of the temples of Ilaiṅgōyil, Tiruvalīsvaram-uḍaiya-Nāyanār and Śrīkayilāsamuḍaiya-Nāyanār. [The date is irregular. Mr. Swamikannu Pillai would place it on Monday, January 28, A.D. 1264, but change the month to Kumbha.]

cells.remarks: On the east wall of the first prākāra of the same temple. Dated in the reign of the Chōla king Rājakēsarivarman alias Chakravartin Kulōttuṅga-Chōladēva I. Records in his thirty-sixth year, Rishabha, śu. di. 3, Saturday, Rōhiṇī (corresponding most probably to Saturday, May 5, A.D. 1106), gift of land to the temple of Tiruvalpōkkimalai-Mahādēva in Kurunāgannāḍu, a subdivision of Rajamahēndra-vaḷanāḍu. The assembly of Kuḷiṭṭandalai, a brahmadēya in Mikōḍu-nāḍu, having met in the hall called Rajēndraśōlan tirumaṇṭapam, made a sale of land to a merchant of Sivapadachēkharapuram who assigned it for the sacred bath of the God in that temple. [The price of the land was 12 kalañjus and 1 kuṇri, of which 5 kalañjus and 1 kuṇri formed the capital for the tax to be paid to Government.]

Records in his twentieth year, Vrischika, ba. di. 8, Monday, Pūrva-Phalguni, gift of 8 anai-achchu for offerings to the image of Ariya Nāyanār. The date corresponded to Monday, November 23, A.D. 1198.

Records sale of land by the assembly to the temple on the hill Tiruvātpōkkimalai. Refers to a revenue survey. Mikōttu-nāḍu is here stated to be in Sarvalōkāśraya-vaḷanāḍu.

cells.remarks: On the rock near a spring behind the Haralākēśvari temple on the same hill. A record of the Chōla king Parakēsarivarman alias Daiyār Śrī-Rājēndra-Chōladēva (I) in his twenty-first year. Records a sale of land by the assembly of Ariñjigai-chaturvēdimangalam, a brahmadēya in Uraiyūrkūṟram, a subdivision of Kēraḷāntaka-vaḷanāḍu. It was probably made in favour of the temple of Śrīkayilāsam alias Madhurāntakaīśvaram at Rājēndra-Chōḷappēttai in Mikōttu-nāḍu. [The cost of 1½ nilam is given as 380 kāśus which included the iraikāval. The dues enumerated are: pecurru, silvaru, yeccoru, vellivedine, kulasambu, seyirvettu unnittu tiruvasalil ponda kudame.]

Under the orders of Ramaraja Vitthalaraja, Timma (his younger brother) made a grant to the God on the hill called Ratnagiri. The composer of this inscription was a certain Dharmaraja of Kakkalur. The date "can be calculated but cannot be verified."

cells.remarks: On the second gōpura of the same temple, left and right of entrance. A damaged record of the Chōḷa king Tribhuvanachakravartin Rājēndra-Chōḷadēva III, dated in his fourth year, Dhanus, su. di. 3, Thursday, Tiruvōṇam. Seems to record an enquiry into the affairs of the temple of Tirumaṇikkamalai-Uḍaiya-Nāyaṉār in Kurukkaināḍu, a subdivision of Rājagambhīra-vaḷanāḍu. The committee of enquiry included the great minister Maṇḍalika Murāri Āliya-Sōmaya-Daṇḍanāyaka, Sēvaya-Daṇḍanāyaka and Sōmanātha Vittaya who was a servant in the place of Sōmēśvaradēva. The mahēśvaras, sthānikas and merchants were also included. Vīraسōmēśvara's appointment of his own men shows that the Chōḷa recognized his suzerainty.]

Records remission of certain taxes in favour of a number of temples. The Sanskrit verse namastuṅga, etc., is written mostly in Tamil. The taxes amounted to 10,000 gold pieces and consisted of four items, viz., "jōdi, śulavari, piravari and araśupēṛu." See also S.A. 435, 233 and Tp. 608 below.

cells.remarks: At the head-sluice of the Periyavāykkāl. A record of Tribhuvanachakravartin Śrī-Rājarājadēva, in his fourth year. Mr. Walhouse gives a description of this in Ind. Antq., Vol. IV, p. 273. His statement that "king Lorakkōṇan" cut the channel is of course, as he himself thought, inaccurate. As a matter of fact it is an inscription of Rājarāja III, dated A.D. 1219. The inscription refers to Musiri as Mummuḍi-Chōlapēṭṭai. See Trichinopoly Gazr., Vol. I, p. 288. Also Antiquities, Vol. I, p. 266.

cells.remarks: On the south wall of the maṇṭapa in front of the same shrine. A mutilated record in the fortysecond year of the Chola king Rājakesarivarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulōttuṅga-Chōḷadēva (1070—1118). Mentions the conquest of Kaliṅga. This is evidently the second Kaliṅga invasion of the reign which took place about A.D. 1111—2 and which is apparently described in the Kaliṅgattupparaṇi. The first invasion took place about 1095-6, an evidence of which we have in the king's inscription at Siṁhāchalam in A.D. 1098-9. Venkayya's theory is that the earlier invasion was in S. Kaliṅga (i.e., Vizagapatam and portion of Gañjām) while the second was against N. Kaliṅga. Both took place when Anantavarman Chōḍagaṅga, Kulōttuṅga's grandson by his daughter Rājasundari, was the ruler (1078-1146). See Ep. Rep., 1905, pp. 52-3. 'See also 44 of 1891 at Alaṅguḍi in the Tanjore district.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 45 of Mr. Sewell's List.—Records grant in Ś. 1714 (A.D. 1792), K. 4839, Paritāpi, by Vijaya Veṅkaṭachala Reḍḍi, of the village of Tiruppanjeri (Tiruppaṅgili) for a Śiva temple, in Turaiyūr. -Tiruppattūr. See Trichinopoly Gazr., p. 290. The local legend is that Subrahmaṇya obtained here the spear with which he killed Śūra. Till the time of the Vijayanagar king Vīra Vijaya this place was known, as epigraphy shows, as Mādhava Chaturvēdimṅgalam, named evidently after Mādhava Daṇḍanāyaka of Daṇāiken-kōṭṭai.

cells.remarks: On the south wall of the same maṇṭapa. A record of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Vira-Pāṇḍyadeva in his twenty-second year, Vrischika, śu. di. 5, Monday, Uttirāḍam. Refers to Perumāḷ Kulaśēkharadēva and to Vijayālayadēva. Records gift of the village of Ūrrakkarai alias Alagiyakūṭṭanallūr in Vaḍagarai Karikalasōlavalanāḍu, to the temple of Kaiyilāsamuḍaiya-Nāyanār at Tirukkarikuḍi alias Vikramasōlapuram, by the residents of that district for the purpose of providing offerings during the festival called Siṟṟirai-tiṟu nāḷ. [Diwan Bahadur Swamikannu Pillai says that either Monday, 5th November 1274, or Monday, 30th October 1318, will suit. In the former case the king was Jaṭāvarman Vīra- Pāṇḍya, the conqueror of Īlam, Koṅgu and Sōlamaṇḍalam and anointer of kings at Perumbarrappuliyūr who ascended the throne in 1253; and in the latter the Vīra Pāṇḍya of the Mussalman times who acceded to the throne A.D. in 1295. Mr. Krishna Sastri identifies him with the latter on the ground that the Visālayadēva of this epigraph was the same as his namesake who reconsecrated the Tiruppattūr temple after the Mussalman invasions.]

cells.remarks: In the monolithic cave forming the central shrine of the Raṅganātha temple on the same hill. Mentions the following birudas: Nāyapara, Prākṛitipriyā, Naravāhana, Utpalakarṇikā, Udārachitta, and refers to the Ati yēndra-Vishṇugṛiha and the Atiyaṅvavāya. The inscription is of great importance in regard to the history of the Adigaimans (Adiyamans, Adiyamas, etc.) who had their capital at Tagaḍūr (Dharmapuri). It shows that their territory extended as far as Nāmakkal. See the inscriptions of Oḍḍappaṭṭi, Dharmapuri, etc., in Salem.

cells.remarks: A C.P. grant (No. 29 of 1906) of Vira-Chola. (See Ind. Antq., Vol. IX, pp. 47--50; Salem Manual, Vol. II, pp. 365--8 and Ep. Ind., Vol. III, pp. 78--82, where it is called Udayendiram plates of Vira-Chola. These contained only two plates. A third was obtained by Venkayya in 1905 and summarized in Ep. Rep., 1906, pp. 74-5. It is in Sanskrit-Grantha and records a grant of Vira- Chola, a Kerala prince but feudatory of a Parakesarivarman-Chola. The inscription shows that the Keralas were in possession of Kongu at this time. Amidst the ancestors of Vira-Kerala we meet with Manikuttuva (who reminds us of Senguttuva of early Tamil literature) and Kodai Ravi (who reminds us of his namesake in Malabar and Kochin epigraphs).

cells.remarks: On the same base. Dated in the reign of the Vijayanagara king Vīrapratāpa Dēvarāya-Mahārāya (II), son of Vīra-Vijayarāya. Records in Ś. 1351, Saumya, Makara, śu. di., Friday, Pūrattāḍi, gift of the village of Adiśūdamaṅgalam with all its income for worship and repairs in the same temple by the residents of Viṭṭappaṛṛu and the community of taṇdirimār. The income from the village included assessment on wet and dry lands, houses and house-sites, peṟkaḍamai, tarikkaḍamai, aṭṭaikhaṇikkai, nāṭṭuviniyōgam, paṭṭirai, pādavari, ālamañji, ariśikāṇam, kōnigai, virimuṭṭu and vanniyavari.

The twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth years of the king are also quoted.

cells.remarks: On the same base. A record of the Pāṇḍya king Tribhuvanachakravartin Parākrama-Pāṇḍyadēva. Refers in his fourth year to some events connected with the temple which happened in the fourth year of Vikrama-Chōḷa and in the reign of Kulōttuṅga-Chōḷa (II) and states that the residents of various divisions met together at Ugalūr and agreed to conduct the worship in the temple as had been done before by their ancestors.

cells.remarks: On the second gōpura of the same temple, right of entrance. Registers in Durmukhi, that the tenants (kuḍi) in twelve villages of Ugalūr-Kurumbarvāy-śīrmai had abandoned them owing perhaps to heavy taxation and consequently an agent of Vīramarāsar, regulated the taxes at five paṇams for the first year and ten from the following year on each plough of dry land and at eight paṇams on every 100 kuḷis of wet land.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 137 of Mr. Sewell's List.—(Tamil.) Records a private grant, no ruler's name being mentioned, by which the inhabitants of seventeen villages agreed to pay every year a tax for the maintenance of the service in the Śiva temple at Āḍuturai, in Ś. 1720 (A.D. 1798), Kālayukti. [This inscription is in the Mack. MSS. See Ins., S. Dts., p. 214, No. 37. It gives the additional information that the grant consisted of one paṇam for every kāṇi of land and ten paṇams for each weaver loom.]

cells.remarks: On the south wall of the central shrine in the Madanagopalasvamin temple. States in the ninth year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Konerinmaikondan that the residents of Vembar-nadu were ordered to collect varam from the varaparru villages and kadamai from kadamaiparru ones. The amount realized by this arrangement was to be spent in making friendly terms with and meeting the expenses of the followers of Sundara-Pandyadeva.

cells.remarks: On the same wall. Registers in his tenth year, an order to the inhabitants of Melkurru-nadu in Vembar-nadu stating that the village Nochchiyam which was once a tax-free village of the temple of Gopalakuttar Vinnagar-Emberuman at Perumbalur was assessed at some later period but was again made tax-free by Kadaladaitta-Perumal alias Sundara-Pandya Vilupparaiyar, a native of Ilaiikudi in Pandi-mandalam.

cells.remarks: On the south base of the same shrine. Remission of jodi in Vyaya, on the village of Nochchiyam by an agent of Krishnappa Nayaka and the residents of Venbarsirmai. The village is stated to have been owned by the temple of Perumal Gopalakuttar at Perumbalur since the time of Dharmaputra. Mentions Surappa-Nayaka in whose time a small amount of jodi used to be collected from that village.

cells.remarks: On the north wall of the same shrine. A damaged record of the Pandya king Perumal Sundara-Pandyadeva, dated in his eighteenth year. Registers that the residents of Perumbalur made a gift of land for celebrating a special festival in the temple on the day of Bharani (Purvashadha), in the month of Purattasi which was the asterism under which, evidently, the queen Tennavanaimuludumudaiyal was born. See No. 255.

cells.remarks: On the same wall. Records in the eighteenth year (of ?) gift of land for maintaining the festival of Akkantirunal which happened on Bharani in the same temple. The document is signed by Sundara Pandya Vilupparaiyan. Evidently this gift is connected with what has been recorded in the above inscription. See No. 255.

cells.remarks: On the same wall. A record of the Pandya king Sundara Pandya, "who conquered all countries." Refers in his eighteenth year to the gift registered of twelve velis of land south of Perumbalur, which had been lying waste for many years by the residents of that village for conducting the festival of Bharani in honour of the birthday of the queen Tennavanaimuludumudaiyal. cells.remarks: On the east wall of the maṇṭapa in front of the central shrine in the Siddharatnēśvara temple. Dated in the reign of the Chōla king Tribhuvanachakravartin Tribhuvanavīradēva (i.e., Kulōttuṅga III). Registers in his fortieth year a compact drawn up by the Śrutimāns of Ūrraṭṭūr, assembled in the maṇṭapa of the temple called Uttamaśōlan for the community of Iḍaṅgai classes who consisted of ninety-eight sub-sects. {The inscription is one of the valuable documents for the construction of the social history of the land. It gives an account of the origin of the Iḍaṅgais, their duties and privileges and their paraphernalia. See Ep. Rep., 1913, p. 109, for a full summary, which is too large to be quoted here. The Śrutimāns were apparently a cultivating section of the Iḍaṅgais.]

cells.remarks: On the same gopura, left of entrance. Records that the Hoysaḷa king Sārvabhaumachakravartin Vīra-Rāmanāthadēva fixed in his seventeenth year the rate of tax on cattle levied in all the eight subdivisions which formed the district of Ūṟṟattūr-nāḍu; but remitted the same on the cattle belonging to the temple of Togumāmaṇi-Nāyaṉār. The taxes consisted of tēn kāśus per year on each sheep, thirty kāśus on each cow and 100 kāśus on each buffalo. The temple tenants were exempted from these.

cells.remarks: On the gopura of the Vriddhachaleśvara temple, right of entrance. A record of the Vijayanagara king Venkatapatideva-Maharaya (II), dated in S. 1545, Rudhirodgarin, Vaiyasi 3, Rishabha, śu. di. 12, Attam, Thursday (= Thursday, 1st May 1623 A.D.). Records that one Linga Reddi of the Pantakula race consecrated the shrines of Palamalainathasvamin and Periyammai-Nachchi at Vriddhachalam alias Veṅganur, presented images, constructed mantapas and gopuras and also made provision for worship and oblations. Mentions Senji in Venbar-nadu which was a subdivision of Karikalakanna valanadu in Magadamandalam. [The inscription seems to show that Venkata II was ruling part of the Empire in the time of Rama IV.]

cells.remarks: On the same gōpura. [The communities mentioned are the Veḷḷāḷas; the Kāśāvargattār including the Kōmuṭṭis, Kaikkōḷars, Śēnias, Sēkkārs, Eruttukkāras, etc.; the Brāhmaṇas; and the Perumakkal of various castes. All these undertook to pay to the temple a fixed rate of grain as soon as they raised crops, besides paṇam on every loom and one paṇam per head to be paid by the Kāśāvargattār each year.]

cells.remarks: In the same place. A damaged record of the Chola king Tribhuvanachakravartin Rajadhirajadeva II, "who was pleased to take Ilam (Ceylon) and . . . ," dated in his thirteenth year. Records that the Siva Brahmanas of Madhurantaka-chaturvedimangalam borrowed some money from the temple treasury, and agreed to burn a lamp in the temple of Kailasamudaiyar, for the interest on the borrowed amount. [Some Siva- Brahmana families deserted their homes and lands this year and ran away. The lands were neglected and the rents unpaid in consequence. Other Siva-Brahmanas of the village met and settled that the lands should be sold to the temple. The Epigraphist ascribes the inscription to Rajadhiraja II and suggests that the trouble at Alambakkam should have been an incident in the course of the war of the Pandyan succession which was fought in his times.]

cells.remarks: On the north wall of the, central shrine in the Uttamar temple. A record in the thirtieth year of the Chōla king Rājaakēsarivarman alias Udaiyār Rājadhirājadēva. Records gift of land. [Uttamar kōvil figures in the Guruparampara of the Teṅgalai Vaiṣṇavites as the scene of the early services of the teacher Nambillai (Varadarāja) or Lōkāchārya. For Nam¬ billai's position in the history of Śrī Vaiṣṇavism in South India, his life, his services to the prabandhic party, his disciples, etc., see my article on the History of Śrī Vaiṣṇavism from the death of Rāmā¬ nuja up to Vēdānta Dēśika in J.Bo.R.A.S., 1914-5.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 50 of Mr. Sewell's List.—(Telugu.) Records grant of land for a charity at the great temple of Śrīraṅgam by Vijaya Rṅga Chokkanātha of the Madura Nāyakkan dynasty in Ś. 1638 (A.D. 1716). The grant mentions his father Raṅga Kṛishṇa Muttuv Virappa, and grandfather Chokkanātha, and states that the Vijaya¬ nagar sovereign Śrī Vīra Raṅga Raya was then reigning at Ghana¬ giri. The recognition of a Vijayanagar ruler is, of course, a mere formality. For a detailed account of the reign of Vijaya Ranga Chokkanatha see Ind. Antq., 1917, September-November.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 27 of 1905-6.—(Telugu.) A record of the Vijayanagara king Vīrapratāpa Dēvarāya Mahārāya (I) in Ś. 1336, Jaya. Records gift of the village of Naruvūru (in Kiḷaṅguṇādu) by the king's son Vīra-Harihararāya-Odeya II to a private individual who, in his turn, gave the village to the temple of Śrīraṅganātha. cells.remarks: On the east wall of the second prākāra of the Raṅganātha temple. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 148—52,

See also my article on Vēdānta Dēśika in J. Bo. R.A.S., 1916.

cells.remarks: On the south wall of the fourth prakara of the same temple. A record of the Chola king Tribhuvanachakravartin Rajendra-Choladeva III, dated in his seventh year. See Ep. Ind., Vol. VII, p. 176, where Kielhorn points out that the date corresponded to Wednesday, December 25, A.D. 1252. The king resided at Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and claims to have defeated the Hoysala king Vira Somesvara, father of Vira Ramanatha, who had inscriptions as far south as Sendalai (57 of 1897) and Mannargudi (85 and 97 of 1897).

Ep. Rep., 1900, p. 30. See Ep. Ind., Vol. VII, p. 177, where Kielhorn points out that the date of the inscription is irregular.

cells.remarks: In the same temple. "An inscription commemorating the self-immolation of a manager of the fane at Śrīrangam whose name was Appana Ayengar. In consequence of all supplies to the fane being withheld, in a bad time, he ascended the Rayer gōpura or lofty tower, and precipitated himself to the ground. The twentyfourth of Tai of a cyclic year only is mentioned. The precise time of the occurrence cannot be, from the document, ascertained. But possibly it is the incident related by Mr. Orme, and by him ascribed to a somewhat different cause." Rais. Catal., Vol. III, p. 311, No. 68.

cells.remarks: On the same wall. Records in the eleventh year (Makara, Purva. 6, Wednesday, Rohini) of the Pandya king Sundara Pandya gift of land by the people of Misenigili-nadu in Tenkarai Jayasinga-kulakala-valanadu. See Ep. Ind., Vol. XI, p. 255, where Mr. R. Sewell points out that the date suits neither the king who ascended the throne in 1251 nor him who came in 1276. [Can it be he who ascended the throne in 1270? Mr. Swamikannu Pillai fixes it on March 5th, A.D. 1264, in the reign of the first of these.]

cells.remarks: On the north wall of the same shrine. A record of Chola king Tribhuvanachakravartin Rajarajadeva (III). Records in his fourth year that a linga was set up in the first prakara of the temple of Nedungalam-Udaiyar under the name Ulaganadisvaram-Udaiyar, for the merit of Tillai Tirunattapperumal alias Vijayalaya Muttaraiyar of Valambakudi, by one of his sons Anapaya Muttaraiyan. Mentions Periyadevar Tribhuvanaviradeva (i.e., Kulottunga III, 1186--1216) and a previous grant by him. So the Rajaraja referred to in this inscription should be Rajaraja III.

cells.remarks: On the same base. An incomplete record of the Chola king Parakesarivarman alias Rajendra- Choladeva I, dated in his fifth year. The last item of conquest is that of Ceylon. The details of the date are Tuesday, the day of Satabhishaj, in Mesha, which, according to Kielhorn, corresponded to Tuesday, 26th March, A.D. 1017. He also infers from this that the reign of Rajendrachola I could not have begun before the 27th March, A.D. 1012. See Ep. Ind., Vol. VIII, pp. 261-2.

cells.remarks: On the same rock. Records in the thirteenth year of the Pāṇḍya king Mārañjadaiyan gift of gold for a lamp to the temple of Tiruvānaikkal- Perumāṇadigaḷ at Tiruvellarai by king Pāṇḍya Mahārāja alias Mārañjaḍaiyan. A portion of the historical introduction of Rājēndra Chōla I is engraved below the inscription. The Government Epigraphist identifies Mārañjaḍaiyan with his namesake of the Trichinopoly cave inscription and Varaguṇa-Pāṇḍya who ascended the throne in A.D. 862. See Ep. Ind., Vol. XI, p. 253, where Mr. Sewell discusses the date and points out that the details (Monday, Aśvini, in Vrischika) corresponded to 22nd November A.D. 874. Mr. Sewell deduces from this that he should have succeeded to the throne between March 22nd and November 22nd, A.D. 862.

cells.remarks: On the north wall of the central shrine in the Ujjīvanāthasvāmin temple. cells.remarks: On the same wall. A record of the Chōḷa king Rājakēsarivarman, dated seventh year, Makara, Tuesday, Ārdrā. Records gift of land for feeding three Śivayōgins and two Brāhmaṇas in the choultry on the sacred hill of the Ālvār at Tiruverumbiyūr. A portion of the inscription is covered by the water cistern. The Epigraphist believes that the Rājakēsarivarman of this inscription is the same as the one referred to in 731, 732, 754, 757 and 760 below and that he should be earlier than Parāntaka I not only on palæographical grounds, but on the ground that these inscriptions refer to the place as Erumbiyūr and not Ten- Kailāsa as in Parāntaka’s records. Mr. Swamikannu Pillai shows from the chronological data of these that there are five possibilities of chronological sequence among them between 850 and 907 A.D., viz., (1) 29th May 866 to 13th January 889; (2) 25th May 869 to 10th January 872; (3) 15th June 886 to 2nd January 889; (4) 30th May 893 to 16th January 896; and (5) 26th May 896 to 11th January 899. See Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 72. So the possible dates of the present inscription are 29th May 866, 25th May 869, 15th June 886, 30th May 893 and 26th May 896. It should thus belong to a Rājakēsarivarman before Parāntaka I,—not improbably Āditya I.

cells.remarks: On the outer row of pillars in the upper rock-cut cave. A partly damaged record. The inscription contains a number of birudas in Sanskrit, a few in Tamil and the rest apparently in Telugu. This inscription seems to have been continued on the pillar forming part of the outer wall of the central shrine to its left, but a few letters only of the first line can now be seen on it. See Ep. Ind., Vol. I, pp. 58--60, where Dr. Hultzsch edits the two inscriptions on the pillar, and also Vol. I, Nos. 33 and 34, pp. 28--30.

cells.remarks: On the pillars on the left side of the same cave. "Each of the two pillars contains four Sanskrit verses which record that a king Gunabhara who bore the birudas Purushottama, Satrumalla and Satyasandha, built a temple of Siva on the top of the mountain and placed in it a linga and statue of himself." The river Kaveri is called the beloved of the Pallava. This together with the palaeographical similarity of this epigraph with the Pallava inscriptions of Mamallapuram and Conjeeveram, made Dr. Hultzsch recognize in Gunabhara, a Pallava king who ruled over the Chola country; and the later researches of Venkayya and others have decided that Gunabhara was the famous Mahendravarman I.]

cells.remarks: On the north, west and south walls of the same shrine. A record of the Chōla king Rājakēsarivarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulōttuṅga-Chōladēva I. Records in his twenty-seventh year, Tulā, śu. di. 10, Sunday, Satabhishaj, corresponding to 18th October 1097, gift of land for a flower garden by the assembly of Kāmaravalli-chaturvēdimangalam, a brahmādēya in Viraikūrram which was a subdivision of Gēyavinōdavaļanādu. The land had been waste and it was now given for the garden tax-free, and the assembly resolved to bear the burden in case the tax (irai) was levied.

cells.remarks: On the third gōpura of the same temple, right of entrance. A record in the twenty-sixth year of the Chōla king Kō-Rajakēsarivarman alias Rājādhirājadēva (I). Records gift of land. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, p. 216, where Prof. Kielhorn points out that the date of the inscription (Wednesday, Uttara Phālguni, at night, month of Mīna) corresponded to Wednesday, the 14th of March, A.D. 1044. The inscription shows that Rājādhirāja ascended the throne in 1018, during the life-time of his predecessor Rājēndra Chōla, whom the people refer to as “our Emperor.” The exact relationship of the two is not known. See No. 279 of 1895 at Mindigal (Kolar district) which corroborates this. 203

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 5 of 1909-10.—A copper-plate grant, dated in Ś. 1662, Rudhirōdgārin, and making a gift to the temple of Poṇṇārmēniyar, which was left unclaimed in the Madras High Court and deposited in the museum. The record is to the effect that three private individuals made over to a certain Kumārasvāmi Paṇḍāram a piece of land situated in Poygaivaḷanāḍu for worship in the temple of Namtambirānār or Poṇṇārmēniyar at Tirumalapāḍi. The trust was conveyed, it is said, in accordance with a previous charter issued by Vijaya Oppilāda Maḷavarāyar of Tirumalai. The Government Epigraphist points out that the Śaka date and the cyclic year do not correspond ; that the inscriptions recorded above do not mention any person as Vijaya Oppilāda Maḷavarāyar; but that Poṇṇārmēniya occurs as a surname of the local deity in a hymn of Sundaramūrti Nāyanār. See Mad. Ep., Rep., 1910, p. 11. I have traced this inscription to the Mack. MSS., Ins., S. Dts., p. 206, No. 12.

cells.remarks: On the east wall of the maṇṭapa in front of the same temple. Records in the thirty-sixth year of the Chōla king Rājakēsarivarman alias Chakravartin Śrī-Kulōttuṅga-Chōladēva (I, 1070-1118) provision for the annual supply of areca-nuts and betel-leaves to the temple of Tirunalakkunramuḍaiya-Mahādēvar. Says that the people of the Raṭṭapāḍikoṇḍachōlavalanaḍu made an agreement with two persons by which, in return for the privilege of levying brokerage on all the betelleaf imported into the district, they should supply 30,000 arecanuts and 750 betel-bundles every year. The people of the district and "the 500 constituting the padai (army) of the district" were to supervise.

cells.remarks: On the cross wall of the east prākāra of the same temple. An inscription of the twelfth year of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Sundara-Pāṇḍyadēva (unidentified). Records that the Araiyars of Iraṇḍu-malaināḍu gave an agreement to the headman of Kuṇṇāṇḍārkōyil that during the times of enmity and war amongst themselves they will in no way molest the tenants and other inhabitants of the villages which they were guarding. "If, however, any person is sainjured they would pay a fine of 100 paṇams and if a village is destroyed they would pay a fine of 500 paṇams. Doing this they still agreed to protect (the villagers and cultivators) though there may be cutting, piercing and dying (in their communal fights)." Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 103.

cells.remarks: Records in the twentieth year of the Chōḷa king Parakēsarivarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulōttuṅga- Chōḷadēva II, the gift of 100 sheep for a lamp. Mr. Swamikannu Pillai calculates the date (Thursday, Sravana, su. di. 11, Kanya) to be Thursday, September 11, A.D. 1152. As the accession of Kulottunga II was between 9th May and 17th August 1133 the present date is in agreement with it. It is the latest date of his reign and shows that it continued into the reign of his successor Rajaraja II whose initial date was 1146.

cells.remarks: On the same entrance. A record of the Chola king Rajakesarivarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulottunga-Choladeva (I ?). cells.remarks: On the same wall. A record of the Chola king Parakesarivarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Tribhuvanaviradeva, "who having taken Ilam (Ceylon), Madurai (Madura) and the crowned head of the Pandya, was pleased to perform the anointment of heroes and the anointment of victors at Madura" (Kulottunga III). Records in his thirty-fifth year the gift of the village Punnaingudi to the temple of Tirupperumananda-Nayanar for worship and repairs by Urudaipperumal alias Edirilisola Kadambarayan for the merit of the king during his stay at Madura. The village was subsequently renamed Udaiyaperumalnallur after the king. Mentions the road Tribhuvanaviranperuvali.

cells.remarks: On the west base of the Amman shrine in the same temple. cells.remarks: Round the top and left side of one of the seventeen beds in the cavern, locally known as Eladipattam. A record in Brahmi. The Government Epigraphist gives the plate and tentative reading of it in Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 86, but no interpretation has been suggested. It is to this effect:— Top. eO mi na t[u] ku mu th[u] [u] ra (?) pi ju na ta ka vu t[i] l te na ku chi tu po[ch]i la l l[a] Left side. Gha (?) ra che [gha] ? l[o] a [Su] ? ta a na ma. “ Other epigraphs found in the adjoining beds in the cavern are engraved in early Tamil characters of about the eighth century A.D. Proper names of six individuals are mentioned " and they " perhaps commemorate the names of mendicants who had resolved to spend the last days of their lives in retired seclusion." Tirugokarnam.

Records a gift of land for a lamp to the temple of Tiruvarankulam-udaiya- Nayanar, by the citizens of Arumolidevapuram in Virudarajabhayankaravalanadu alias Kananadu. Mentions the coin called Valalvali-tirandan panam. [The identity of the king is not known. The Government Epigraphist identifies the king with his namesake figuring in Tj. 476 and 478. According to the former of these (which gives astronomical details, which have been examined by Mr. Swamikannu Pillai in Mad. Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 77) he has to be identified with Jatavarman Sundara Pandya who came to the throne on the 24th June 1276. But the irregularity of the chronology of the latter makes the identity somewhat suspicious. No. 139 above refers to the same king. See also No. 246 above for probably the same king.]

cells.remarks: On the east wall of the same mantapa. Dated in the reign of the Chola king Tribhuvanachakravartin Tribhuvanaviradeva (i.e., Kulottunga III), “who having taken Madurai (Madura), Ilam (Ceylon), Karuvur and the crowned head of the Pandya was pleased to perform the anointment of heroes and the anointment of victors at Madura.” Records in his fortieth year Karkataka that the assembly of the inhabitants of Vallanadu met together and bound themselves to protect the cultivators (kudimakkal) of this and other devadana villages. “If any one of the assembly was found to rob, capture the cows, or do other mischief to cultivators, the assembly agreed to assign two mas of wet land to the temple by way of fine for the offence committed. Also the Settis, Kaikkolars, smiths and shepherds and others of the sacred village who had acquired lands, wet or dry, from the assembly, were allowed to enjoy them on permanent lease and pay their dues direct to the temple." Ep. Rep., 1915, pp. 99-100. [Mr. Krishna Sastri believes that the inscription affords an evidence of the disturbed state of the Chola dominions in this reign.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 14 of 1908-9.—A grant of the Eastern Chālukya Vishṇuvardhana Bhīma I, discovered in this village. It gives the usual genealogy of the dynasty and says that the king who conquered his dāyādas, including the Rāshtrakūṭa Krishna II, granted a village in Elamañcha Kaliṅgadēśa and Dēvarāshtra Vishaya. The grant is incomplete. Elamañchi was perhaps the capital. The grant gives the last verse of Bhavabhūtis Mālatimādhava, thereby showing that Bhavabhūti lived before Chālukya Bhīma I. [Dēvarāshṭra Vishaya is mentioned in the Allahabad pillar inscription o Samudragupta. See Fleet's Corpus Ins. Indic., Vol. III, p. 13.] Ep. Rep., 1909, pp. 108-9.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 10 of 1908-9.--(Sanskrit in old Telugu character.) A grant of the Eastern Chālukyan (?) king Kokilivarma Mahārāja or (Kakkuli Mahārāja) who had the titles of Sarvalokāśraya and Anivāritasaktitrayasampanna. Records grant of a village called Boḍḍeri in Bhōgipura Vishaya, in Madhyama Kaliṅga, to a Brahman of Muñjeṛu on the day of a lunar eclipse. It was made by the king from his residence at Elamañchi, the modern Yellamañchili, in Sarvasiddhi taluk. [Kokili is said to be the son BİMLİPAṬAM TALUK 1667 of Vinayādityavārman and grandson of Mangivarman. The introductory portions of the epigraph are like those of the Eastern Chālukyan kings Vishnuvardhana I, Jayasiṃha I, Vishnuvardhana II and Mangiyuvarāja. These together with the title Sarvalokāśraya, show that the king was an early Eastern Chālukya.]

Like every such chief he had the titles of Sarvalokāśraya, Dharanīvarāha, etc. For Kumārayarrama see No. 27 below.

cells.remarks: On a third pillar in the asthānamaṇṭapa of the Dharmaliṅgeśvara temple. Dated in the reign of the Eastern Chāḷukya Nrisimha. Records in Ś. 1350 (A.D. 1428) a genealogy of the king and records that his queen Vīrāmbā built a tank called Vīrasāgara and that he himself built the antarālamaṇṭapa of the temple. This and No. 28 below introduce a distinct branch of the Eastern Chāḷukyas, which traces its descent from a Vijayāditya “ who was born in the family of Kulōttuṅga I.” From Vijayāditya to Nrisimha of the present epigraph there were twelve generations.* All these chiefs bore the Eastern Chāḷukyan titles of Sarvalokāśraya and Vishṇuvardhana. * The genealogy is as follows:— Vijayāditya (= Chaṇḍāmbikā) I Mallapa I (= Lakshmi) I Upendra I (= Gaṅgāmbā) I Malla II (= Chōḍāmbā) I Upendra II (= Mallāmbā) Founded Chōḍamallāgrahāra and a tank in the name of his father in Ś. 1205. cells.remarks: On the west face of the same pillar. Kumarayarrama records in Ś. 1354, Parīdhāvin, gift of a lamp. cells.remarks: On the south, east and north faces of a pillar in the kalyāṇamaṇṭapa of the same temple. The Eastern Chāḷukya king Viśvēśvara records in Ś. 1329 that he built the maṇṭapa in which the pillar is found. Contains a genealogy of the king as in 26 above. See the genealogical tree in p. 1669 for the relative position of Viśvēśvara and Nṛsiṁha. Poet Vinnakōṭa Peddanna, son of Gōvindarāja and author of the Kāvyalaṅkārachūḍāmaṇi dedicates his work to Viśvēśvara and so was his contemporary. [Vīrēśaḷiṅgam Pantulu misreads the inscription and so arrives at a date which is earlier by a century. See his Telugu Poets, Vol. I, pp. 98-99.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 2 of 1907-8.— The Timmapuram plates of Viṣṇuvardhana I, edited by Dr. Hultzsch in Ep. Ind., Vol. IX, pp. 317—9. The inscription is in Sanskrit and records that Viṣṇuvardhana (I) surnamed Viṣamasiddhi, the younger brother of Satyāśraya Vallabha Mahārāja, son of Kīrtivarman, grandson of Raṇavikrama of the (Western) Cāḷukya family, while residing at Piṣṭapuram (Pīṭhāpuram, Gōdāvari district) gave some land at a village called Kumūlūra in the Pālaki-viṣaya to forty Brāhmaṇas. [The donor is the founder of the Eastern Cāḷukyan dynasty. See No. 16 above. Pulakēśin II captured Piṣṭapura and made his brother viceroy over it, thereby founding the eastern branch of the dynasty, about A.D. 634. See Ep. Ind., Vol. VI, p. 61 and Mad. Ep. Rep., 1908, p. 61.]

cells.remarks: A C.P. grant of the Matsya king Arjuna (now deposited in the Madras Museum). It is in Sanskrit language and Telugu characters and records that on Saturday, the Akshaya tritiya of Vaiśākha in Ś. 1191, corresponding to 6th April 1269, the king Arjuna gave, for the spiritual welfare of his father Jayanta, the village of Drubbiḍi (which he re-named Jayanta-Nārāyaṇa) to certain Brāhmaṇas. The full genealogy of the line is given, Arjuna being the twenty-third in descent from Gaṅga the founder. See Ep. Ind., Vol. V, pp. 106—12, for the full edition of the record.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 4 of 1912-13.--A C.P. grant of the Eastern Gaṅga Mahārāja Dēvēndravarman, son of Guṇārṇava, dated in Kaliṅgaṅka' era 195, Śrāvaṇa, ba. di. 5, Dakshiṇāyana. Records gift of land in the village Siddhārtaka to a Brāhmaṇa named Tamparaśarma Dīkshita, a resident of Eraṇḍapalli. [Only one C.P. of this king has been thus far edited. See Ep. Ind., Vol. III, 130 f. It is dated in the year 183 of the same era. The village Siddhārtaka VIZAGAPATAM TALUK' 1675 figures in the Achyutapuram plates of Indravarman also.¹ Ep. Ind., Vol. III, p. 127. "Eraṇḍapalli is perhaps identical with Eraṇḍapalla, whose chief Damana was captured and liberated by the Gupta king Samudragupta in or about the fourth century A.D."² Simhachalam. See Antiquities, Vol. I, p. 16, and Vizag. Manual, p. 70, for the history of the place. Mr. Sewell gives six inscriptions here, but the following is a more detailed and accurate list.

cells.remarks: Above the southern entrance into the kalyāṇamaṇḍapa of the Lakshmīnarasimhasvāmin temple. Records in Ś. 1188, that Lakshmīdevī, wife of a certain Maṅgirāja, granted two lamps for the merit of her son Upendrarāja. [The genealogy of the Pañchadhārla branch of the Eastern Chalukyas seems to show that Maṅgirāja was the same as Mallapa I, the father of Upendra I.]

cells.remarks: On a round pillar in the āsthānamaṇṭapa of the same temple. Records in Ś. 1526, Krōdhin, in the reign of Hajarati-Mahamada-Khulli-Kutubu-Padasaha-Vodaya gift of the village of Narava to Nṛsiṁha of Siṁhadri by Padmanāyaka Sarvappa-Āśvarāyaniṅgāru. This chief, under orders from the Mussalman king, drove Mukunda-Bāhubalīndra beyond the boundary. It is also stated that he granted the village of Kūrmam (i.e., Śrīkūrmam) to the temple and to the Vaishṇavas of that place. [Venkayya identifies Mukunda with Mukunda Harichandana, the Telugu usurper of the Gajapati sovereignty about 1565. See Gz. 250.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 219 of Mr. Sewell's List.—(Telugu and Kanarese.) This grant and Nos. 212 and 213 must be read together. "The series is very interesting, partly because the dynasty referred to is entirely unknown, and partly because we have here grants of the same sovereign in two different alphabets. The date is the end of the eleventh and beginning of the twelfth century A.D.; the place Kaliṅgapatam, or its neighbourhood on the east coast of the peninsula not far south of Orissa." It records the grant by Anantavarma Choḍagaṅga (whose abhiṣheka took place in Ś. 999) in A.D. 1119, of the village of Tāmaraśuṇthi, in the Samva country, to a Brahman named Mādhava. The epigraph gives an elaborate genealogy of the dynasty which is more detailed than, and in some respects different from, that in the above record.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 16 of 1908-9.—A C.P. grant (received from Narasapatam taluk) of the Eastern Gaṅga king Vajrahasta III (1038 ---1070). Registers the grant of the district of Gaurasatta Vishaya (which consisted of 35 villages) to a certain Mānadātiya Choṭṭa, who was the grandson of Choṭṭa Choḍaparāja who had a Vaidumba princess as his wife. The donee was thus highly connected with the royal family. The grant was made from Dantipura in Ś. 967. [The present epigraph is the earliest of Vajrahasta III's grants. The two others are Gj. 143-A and Me. 188.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 15 of 1908-9.—(Sanskrit.) A grant of Indravarman of the Vishṇukuṇḍin family, noticed in Mad. Ep. Rep., 1908-9, p. 110, and Ep. Ind., Vol. XII, pp. 133—6. Records that king Indravarman granted in his twenty-seventh year to a Brahman the village of Peruvātaka in Plakirāshtra. Indravarman was the son of Vikramēndra I and grandson of Mādhavarman of the Vishṇukuṇḍin family. His son Vikramēndravarman II was the donor of the Chikkulla plates (Gd. 365). His power is attested by the fact that he had a capital as far south as Dendalūru in Ellore taluk while his father's capital was Purāṇisaṅgama, somewhere in Vizagapatam district. The lion was the royal emblem of the Vishṇukuṇḍins.

cells.remarks: The Paliyam plates of the 322nd year of the Puduvaippu era. These belong to the " Palayattu Āchchan of Chēndamaṅgalam in the Cochin State; the members of this family were the hereditary ministers of the Rājas of Cochin, but lost their position after the transportation to Madras of one of the Valiya Āchchans who joined the insurgents headed by Vēlu Tambi, Dalavāy of Travancore " in the war of the latter against Cochin and the British resident Macaulay. The epigraph is in Vaṭṭeḷuttu and the date is 14th Mīnam in 322 of the Puduvaippu era, i.e., 22nd March A.D. 1663 (as the Puduvaippu era commemorates the appearance of the island of Vypeen from the sea in 1341). The inscription records an agreement between the royal family of Cochin and the Dutch--the first of its kind--as against internal and external enemies (like the Portuguese). For the terms and details see Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, No. IV. For the war between Paliyattu Āchchan and the English see Trav. Manual, Vol. I, p. 433.

cells.remarks: In the hands of the local Jews. A C.P. grant of Bhāskara Ravivarman which is edited by Dr. Hultzsch in Ep. Ind., Vol. III, pp. 66--70. It is a record in Chēra-Pāṇḍya Vaṭṭeḷuttu and in Tamil language of ordinary, colloquial type, throwing incidental light on the development of the Tamil language into Malayalam. It records that Bhāskara Ravivarman Kōgōṇmaikoṇḍān gave to Issuppu Iṟappan (Joseph Rabban) and descendants in his thirtyeighth year, the village of Añjuvaṇṇam (the quarter of the five classes of artisans ?) at Muyirikkōḍu (Cranganore) together with the 72 proprietary rights, the tolls on elephants and other riding animals and balances, etc., besides various paraphernalia (which are enumerated). [Venkayya believes that the king is the same as the donor of the Tirunelli plates. Joseph Rabban was probably a member of the old Jewish colony at Cranganore, which, in later times, migrated to Cochin on account of Portuguese oppression. The record exists also in Hebrew translation. Dr. Burnell attributes it to the eighth century at latest. According to Mr. Swamikannu Pillai Bhaskara Ravivarman came to the throne in A.D. 978. See Tvc. 180 below. For other editions of the present plate see Madras Journal, Vol. XIII, Part I, p. 135 ff.; Ibid., Vol. II, p. I ff.; Ibid., Vol. XXI, p. 42 f.; Ind. Antq., Vol. XIII, p. 334 and Malabar Manual, Vol. II, pp. CXV ff.]

cells.remarks: A C.P. grant of the Pallava king Nripatungavarman. It is both in Sanskrit and Tamil and records that Nripatunga, the son of Nandivarman (III) and Sankha (of the Rashtrakuta family) gave, at the request of his minister, three villages to a college (vidyasthana) at Bahur. The Tamil portion is dated in the eighth year of Ko-Vijaya-Nripatungavarman and says that he is a devoted Vaishnavite. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 180-1, where a summary of the plates is given by Dr. Hultzsch. [The plates were discovered by Mr. J. Delaton and sent to Paris. Dr. Hultzsch's summary is based on a pandit's version of the epigraph. The text alone is given in S.I.I., Vol. II, p. 514 and a translation of the Sanskrit portion in Prof. J. Dubreuil's Pallavas, pp. 48--51. This is Prof. Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 652.

cells.remarks: A Pallava copper-plate grant (discovered in 1879 and published in S.I.I., Vol. II, No. 73, pp. 342—61). It is in Grantha and Tamil, similar to the Kūram plates, and records the grant of a village by the Pallava king Nandivarman II, the successor of Paramēśvaravarman II. [According to the Udayēndiram plates Nandi was the son of Paramēśvaravarman, but the present epigraph attributes his accession to the popular choice as he was apparently only a remote kinsman. For, he was the son of Hiranya by Rōhiṇī and belonged to the branch of Bhīma, the younger brother of Simhavishṇu. See S.I.I., Vol. II, p. 344, where Dr. Hultzsch gives the genealogy of this line side by side with the Pallava genealogy proper.] The village granted was Koḍukolli or Ekadhīramangalam in Urrukkāṭṭu-kōṭṭam in Toṇḍakāshṭra (i.e., Toṇḍamaṇḍalam) in Chingleput district. The donee was a Brahman named Jyēshṭhapāda Sōmayājin of the Bhāradvāja gōtra and Chhāndōgya Sūtra who was a resident of Puṇḍi (Pūṇiya). The gift was made at the instance of the king's Prime Minister Brahmaśrīrāja. See Prof. Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 635.

cells.remarks: Mr. Nagam Aiya gives two pillars at Kumārimuttam, one of which contains an epigraph, dated in K.A. 669, and granting the harbour dues to the local Roman Catholic Church. The other records an edict issued by Bhūtalavīra Udaya Mārtāṇḍavarman in K.A. 701 (20th Mīnam), i.e., A.D. 1526, safeguarding the rights and privileges of the Christian Parava fishermen of Kumārimuttam harbour who were ill-treated by the Hindu fishermen. It is addressed to the senior and junior Kaṅgan of the latter, commanding them not to molest the Christians " who were exempted from paying the taxes due to the village . . . such as iḍaṅkai, valaṅkaipaṇam, paḍaippaṇam and prachaṇḍakaṇikkai." Trav. Manual, Vol. I, p. 296 and pp. 195-96.

cells.remarks: The Syrian Christian plates of Sthanu Ravi No. I.--(Vatteluttu of "about the latter half of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century A.D.") Records that in the fifth year of king Sthanu Ravi, Aiyanadigal, the Governor of Venadu, gave a number of families of the Ilavars, Ilakkaiyars and Vannans to the church called Tarisappalli at Kurukkeni kollam (i.e., Quilon) by a certain Iso Tapir. These families were freed, on the occasion, from the necessity to pay the taxes of talaikkanam, enikkanam, manaimeypankollum-irai, menippon, polippon, iravuchchoru and kudanali. The converts were also given the privilege of taking their carts to markets within the fort and of being administered justice by the church authorities. [This epigraph together with the next, mistaken for a single one, was edited by Dr. Gundert in Mad. Jour., Vol. XIII, pp. 115--42, and by Kukkil Kelu Nayar in the same journal. The former has been reproduced in Malabar Manual, Vol. II. It has now been edited by Mr. Gopinatha Rao in Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 60--70, with a history of the plates and detailed explanations of the technical terms occurring therein.

cells.remarks: The Syrian Christian plates of Sthanu Ravi No. II. These are fragmentary and wanting in the first part. The earlier portion is in Vatteluttu and ends with signatures of witnesses in Pahlavi, Kufic and Hebrew. The Vatteluttu of the record is apparently of a later date, but the contents are practically the same as in 89 and so they might be a copy of the latter. The inscription begins with an enumeration of the gift to Tarisappalli of some additional families of professional men like carpenters, Vellalas, etc., and passes on to the gift of lands, the boundary of which was determined by the limit of an elephant's walk. The gift was made by Aiyanadigal Tiruvadi and Rama Tiruvadi, Governor of Venadu, in consultation with the Koyiladhikari and others. The foreign settlers should not be accused of any misdeed and in case they were, they were to be tried and punished by the churchmen only. The document then proceeds to enumerate the fiscal arrangements made for the upkeep of the church and the terms are very informing in regard to the taxation of the age. See Ibid., pp. 70--85.

The inscription begins with an enumeration of the gift to Tarisappalli of some additional families of professional men like carpenters, Vellalas, etc., and passes on to the gift of lands, the boundary of which was determined by the limit of an elephant's walk. The gift was made by Aiyanadigal Tiruvadi and Rama Tiruvadi, Governor of Venadu, in consultation with the Koyiladhikari and others. The foreign settlers should not be accused of any misdeed and in case they were, they were to be tried and punished by the churchmen only. The document then proceeds to enumerate the fiscal arrangements made for the upkeep of the church and the terms are very informing in regard to the taxation of the age. See Ibid., pp. 70--85.

cells.remarks: The Kottayam plate of Vira Raghava. This inscription which is in the hands of the local Syrian Christians is both in Malayalam and Vatteluttu characters. The Vatteluttu is believed by Venkayya to be modern; much more modern than that of the Tirunelli and Cochin plates of Bhaskara Ravivarman. The language of the epigraph is in Tamil prose (mixed with a few Malayalam forms). It records that Vira Raghava Chakravartin who claims to be. a lineal descendant of Vira Kerala Chakravartin conferred, on Saturday, Mina 22, Rohini (when Jupiter was in Makara), the title of Manigramam and certain honours and rights to one Iravikkorran of Magōdaiyarpattipam (Kodungōlūr). The oil-mongers and the five classes of artisans were made his dependents and their dues to him are enumerated. Venkayya interprets Manigramam to be a trading corporation. Burnell attributes the inscription to the eighth century (A.D. 774). Indian astrologers ascribe it to A.D. 230. But Venkayya would assign it to the fourteenth century A.D. and surmises that Vira Raghava might be the same as Jayasimha Vira Keralavarman, the father of Ravivarman Kulasekhara of the Arulalapperumal and Ranganatha inscriptions. Keilhorn accepts Venkayya's date and says that 15th March, A.D. 1320, is intended. The inscription is of high value for the construction of the social and economic history of the age. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 270-7. Also Ep. Ind., Vol. II, pp. 83-84. Ind. Antq., Vol. VI, p. 83. For earlier editions see Madras Journal, Vol. XIII, Part I, p. 118-f. (reprinted in Malabar Manual, Appendix XII, p. CXVII f.; Madras Journal, Vol. XXI, pp. 35-8. See also Trav. Manual, Vol. I, p. 244 and Vol. II, pp. 125-7.

cells.remarks: (Vaṭṭeḷuttu.) On the same boulder. A record in the fifteenth year of the Chola king Kō-Rājarājakēsarivarman. Records that the members of the Mūlaparadai sabhā felt themselves unable to collect the rent and otherwise manage. the affairs of the temple and handed over the charge to the local mahāsabhā who appointed two vāriyars and a kāraṇattān for the purpose. The record is dated on Tuesday, 13th of Kanni, Pūrvashādha, which, according to. Dr. Kielhorn, corresponded to 29th August, A.D. 999. See Ep. Ind., Vol. V, pp. 45--8 and Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 1--8, where Mr. Gopinatha Rao identifies Kāndalūr with a part of Trevandram. His interpretation of the destruction of the śālai as the destruction of a feeding-house seems to me to be absurd.

cells.remarks: A C.P. plate of Rājaśēkhara who bore the imperial titles Śrīrāja, Rājādhirāja, Paramēśvara, etc. In the Vaṭṭeḽuttu alphabet "not later than the ninth century nor earlier than the eighth century." Records that under the king's presidency the people of the eighteen nāḍus of Tiruvarruvāy and of Valaippalli met and made some arrangement regarding the bali ceremony, saying that those who stood in the way should be fined. [Mr. Gopinatha Rāo discusses the date of the king and concludes that he should have lived in the beginning of the ninth century, that he should have been a predecessor of the poet Rājaśēkhara who, he argues, was 215 a king of Kerala, a contemporary of Ranavigraha of the Kalachuri dynasty and so lived in the tenth century. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 8-3, for the full arguments.]

cells.remarks: On the west and south bases of the central shrine of the Vishnu temple at Tirukkadittanam (two miles east of Sengnaseri), one of the thirteen sacred places of Vaishnavism in Malainadu. Records that in the fourteenth year of Bhaskara Ravivarman Govardhana Marttanda, Governor of Vemadu, made certain gifts to the temple. [Marttanda figures in Tirunelli plates as one of the king's feudatories. Bhaskara succeeded to the throne in A.D. 978, according to the calculations of Mr. Swamikannu Pillai. His territories evidently included British Malabar, Cochin and half of Travancore and were divided into various nadus. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 32-3.]

cells.remarks: On the north and west walls of the central shrine. (Vatteluttu.) Dated in the fifteenth year of Bhaskara Ravivarman (A.D. 992). Records that the uralar (townsmen), parudaiyar (member of the parishad), etc., were not to be corrupt in the management of the shrine and collection of rents, that the temple priests should be appointed for three years only, that the expenditure on feeding the Brahmans, the reciters of the Mahabharata, etc., should not be diverted into other channels, and that penalty for failure was a fine of 12 kalanjus and 5 kanams. See the above epigraph and Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 34-8.

cells.remarks: On the two bases of the Tulābhārakkal in the Padmanābhasvāmi temple. (Tamil.) Dated in K. 4702, K.A. 776, when Saturn stood in the Tulārāśi and Jupiter in Kanyārāśi, on Saturday, 12th Mithuna, nakshatra Punarvasu, which have been equated to 20th June, A.D. 1601. Records that king Vīra Ravivarman performed the Tulāpurusha ceremony and his two queens built a maṇṭapa in commemoration of the event. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 28—30.

cells.remarks: The Trevandram Huzur office plates of Kōkkaruṇandadakkan. (Tamil language and alphabet.) Records that on 1449087th day of the Kali era, and fifteenth day of the ninth year of king Karuṇandadakkan, he purchased from the Sabhā of Miñchirai a plot of land, erected a Vishnu temple on it together with a śālai for 95 śaṭṭars (scholars) and endowed lands for temple services, lamps, festivals, etc. The king must have ascended the throne about A.D. 855-6. He belonged to the Yādava or Āykula dynasty who ruled over the mountain tracts of South Travancore who had Āyakūḍi for their capital and who were called the Lords of the Poḍiya mountain. Mr. Gopinatha Rao traces the history of the Āy king Andiran as far as it is ascertained from the Purānānūru. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, p. 3. He also points out that Karuṇandadakkan of these plates should be the same as Aḍakkan or Śrī Vallabha, the son of Karuṇandan and grandson of Saḍayan, and contemporary of Varaguṇa Pāṇḍya, who came to the throne in A.D. 862. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, pp. 1—14 and No. 2 above.

cells.remarks: The Huzur office plate of Vikramāditya Varaguṇa. (Tamil.) The record belongs to the eighth year of king Vikramāditya Varaguṇa and says that while staying at Tirunandikarai he married Murugan Seṇḍi or Āykula Mahādēvi, the daughter of Teṅganāḍu Kiḷavan, and granted some lands for her enjoyment. Mr. T. A. Gopinatha Rao gives arguments to show that this king was the successor of Kōkkaruṇandadakkan referred to in the previous inscription. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, No. II.

cells.remarks: On the slab set up in the southern side of the western gate of the museum. (Vaṭṭeḽuttu.) Belongs to the twenty-seventh year of the Pāṇḍya king Mārañjaḍaiyan and records that in the battle of Viḷiṇam the Pāṇḍya army left the Chēra's in confusion and retired to the fort of Karaikkōṭṭai, and that the Chēra army, rallying themselves, again attacked the Karaikkōṭṭai fort. In the course of this a servant of the Pāṇḍyan king named Raṇakīrti fell struck by an arrow. See Trav. Manual, Vol. I, pp. 182-3 and Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, pp. 153-9, where Mr. Gopinatha Rao gives arguments to prove that the king should be identical with the Mārañjaḍaiyan of the Anaimalai records who lived about A.D. 770.

THE BRITISH MUSEUM. 1721 THE BRITISH MUSEUM. The following inscriptions which belong to the Madras Presidency are at present in the British Museum. I give them here for the sake of convenience. The list may be incomplete. 1. The British Museum * (formerly Sir W. Elliot's) plates of Sadāsiva Rāya. (Sanskrit in Nandināgari character.) Records at the request of Rāmarāja, the ruler of the Karnāta kingdom, who in turn was requested by Kondarāja, descendant of Aravīdu Bukka (in S. 1478, Nala, Māsi, Mrigasirsha, Sunday, new-moon, solar eclipse), the grant of many villages to the great sage Rāmānuja in the presence of God Vitthalēśvara, on the banks of the Tungabhadra. The record gives the genealogy of Sadāsiva as well as the other donors and an elaborate list of the political divisions. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 1-22, where Dr. Kielhorn edits the inscription. The date is irregular. 2. The Nellore district (formerly Sir W. Elliot's, now British Museum?) plates of the second year of the Eastern Chālukyan king Vishnuvardhana II Vishamasiddhi, the grandson of Vishnuvardhana I and son of Indra Bhattaraka, the younger brother of Jayasimha I. The record is dated in S. 586, Chitra, Sukla 10, Maghā, Wednesday, corresponding to 13th March A.D. 664. See Ind. Antq., Vol. VII, p. 186 and Vol. VIII, p. 320. See also Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 550. 3. The Mattewāda first and second plates of the fifth year of the king referred to in the above epigraph, in S. 589, Phālguna, amāvāsya, solar eclipse, corresponding to 17th February A.D. 668. See Ind. Antq., Vol. VII, p. 191 and Ibid., Vol. XX, p. 9. See also Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 551. 4. The British Museum (formerly Sir W. Elliot's) plates of the Eastern Chālukya king Vijayāditya II Narēndramriga Rāja, son of Vishnuvardhana IV and grandson of Vijayāditya I, who, on the occasion of a lunar eclipse, gave the village of Korraparru to twenty-four Brahmans. The dūtaka of the grant was the king's brother Nripa-Rāma, born, it is said, in the Haihaya family. See S.I.I., Vol. I, No. 35, pp. 31-6, and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 553. 5. The Ahadanakaram Sanskrit and Telugu plates of the Eastern Chālukya king Vishnuvardhana V, son of Vijayāditya II, and grandson of Vishnuvardhana IV. See Ind. Antq., Vol. XIII, p. 186, and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 555. 6. THE BRITISH MUSEUM. 1721  THE BRITISH MUSEUM.  The following inscriptions which belong to the Madras Presidency are at present in the British Museum. I give them here for the sake of convenience. The list may be incomplete.  1. The British Museum * (formerly Sir W. Elliot's) plates of Sadāsiva Rāya. (Sanskrit in Nandināgari character.) Records at the request of Rāmarāja, the ruler of the Karnāta kingdom, who in turn was requested by Kondarāja, descendant of Aravīdu Bukka (in S. 1478, Nala, Māsi, Mrigasirsha, Sunday, new-moon, solar eclipse), the grant of many villages to the great sage Rāmānuja in the presence of God Vitthalēśvara, on the banks of the Tungabhadra. The record gives the genealogy of Sadāsiva as well as the other donors and an elaborate list of the political divisions. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 1-22, where Dr. Kielhorn edits the inscription. The date is irregular.  2. The Nellore district (formerly Sir W. Elliot's, now British Museum?) plates of the second year of the Eastern Chālukyan king Vishnuvardhana II Vishamasiddhi, the grandson of Vishnuvardhana I and son of Indra Bhattaraka, the younger brother of Jayasimha I. The record is dated in S. 586, Chitra, Sukla 10, Maghā, Wednesday, corresponding to 13th March A.D. 664. See Ind. Antq., Vol. VII, p. 186 and Vol. VIII, p. 320. See also Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 550.  3.
